---
title: Why Is a Hermitian Product Defined That Way?
---

## What

A Hermitian inner product is a generalization of an inner product for
complex vector spaces.

Like a normal inner product, it's a map:

$$
\langle \cdot , \cdot \rangle : V \times V \to V
$$

It's $\mathbb{R}$-linear on each argument.

$$
\begin{gathered}
\langle u + v, w \rangle = \langle u, w \rangle + \langle v, w \rangle  \\
\langle u, v + w \rangle = \langle u, v \rangle + \langle u, w \rangle
\\
\langle x u, v \rangle = x \langle u, v \rangle  = \langle u, x v \rangle
\quad \text{for } x \in \mathbb{R}
\end{gathered}
$$

And positive definite.

$$
\langle u, u \rangle > 0 \quad \text{for } u \neq 0
$$

But then the definition gets weird.   Instead of being symmetric, it's
conjugate-symmetric, and only only $\mathbb{C}$-linear on the first argument.

$$
\begin{gathered}
\langle z u, v \rangle = z \langle u, v \rangle  \quad \text{for } z \in \mathbb{C} \\
\langle u, v \rangle = \overline{\langle v, u \rangle}
\end{gathered}
$$

Usually, the only justification you'll get when this is introduced is to say that
it has to be this way for the norm $\|v\|^2 = \langle v, v \rangle$ to be real,
because if it were linear in each argument, you could multiply $v$ by $e^{i\theta/2}$
and get any complex phase you want on $\|v\|^2$.

This is true, but it still seems weird to me.  They say you'll get used to it.
I got used to it, but for a long time, I still wished for some better justification
than that.

## Why

All a Hermitian inner product is, is a real inner product, which is compatible with
a complex structure.

What do I mean by that?

A complex vector space can be thought of as a real vector $V$ space with one additional
bit of structure: a map  $J : V \to V$ such that $J^2 = -1$.   Then multiplication
by a complex scalar is defined as:

$$
(a + bi)v = av + b Jv
$$

So, let's say we have a real vector space $V$ and we have two additional bits of
structure:  A complex structure $J$, and a inner product $(\cdot, \cdot)$.
The least you could ask for to say these two structures are "compatible" is that $J$ doesn't
change the norm of a vector.
$$
\|Jv\| = \|v\|
$$

Well, if you have that, you have a Hermitian product, you just didn't know it yet.


::: {#prp-j-preserves-inner-product}
$(Ju, Jv) = (u, v)$ for any vectors $u, v$
:::

::: {.proof}
$$
\begin{align*}
\|u + v\|^2 & = (u + v, u + v) = \|u\|^2 + 2(u,v) + \|v\|^2 \\
= \|J(u + v)\|^2 & = (Ju + Jv, Ju + Jv) = \|Ju\|^2 + 2(Ju,Jv) + \|Jv\|^2 \\
 &= \|u\|^2 + 2(Ju,Jv) + \|v\|^2
\end{align*}
$$
:::


::: {#prp-j-skew-adjoint}
$(u, Jv) = -(Ju, v)$ for any vectors $u, v$
:::

::: {.proof}
$$
(u, Jv) = (Ju, JJv) = (Ju, -v) = -(Ju, v)
$$
:::


::: {#prp-complex-norm}
$\|zu\| = |z| \|u\|$ for any $z \in \mathbb{C}$
:::

::: {.proof}
Let $z = a + bi$ for real $a, b$
$$
\begin{align*}
\|zu\|^2 = (au + bJu, au + bJu) &= a^2\|u\|^2 + b^2\|u\|^2 + (au,bJu) + (bJu, au) \\
&= a^2\|u\|^2 + b^2\|u\|^2 + \cancel{ab(u,Ju)} + \cancel{ab(Ju, u)} \\
&= (a^2 + b^2) \|u\|^2 \\
&= |z|^2 \|u\|^2
\end{align*}
$$
:::

Great! Now it almost looks like we have everything we could have wanted.
We have a norm on our vector space, it's defined by a real-bilinear,
positive-definite inner product.

The product itself isn't complex-linear.  It's not even complex-valued.
It's real valued on all inputs in our complex vector space.

But why should it be complex valued?  The point of this thing is to define a 
norm, right?  And norms are real.  And this norm responds to multiplication by 
a complex factor in exactly the way we expect.  So maybe we don't need the
Hermitian product at all.  Maybe this is a different, better way to
generalize an inner product from real to complex spaces.

Let's investigate the properties that this new kind of product has.

I wonder what angle $u$ makes with $Ju$.  Well, $(u, Ju) = -(Ju, u)$ by
@prp-j-skew-adjoint, but $(u, Ju) = (Ju, u)$ by symmetry.  So the product 
is zero.  They're orthogonal.  I guess that makes sense.  After all, $1$ 
and $i$ are orthogonal to each other on the complex plane.

Still, it is a little bit odd.  That's not the way things work in the 
Hermitian world, where $iu$ is parallel to $u$.

We know what arbitrary complex scalars do to the norm, but what do they do 
to the product in general?

On the right
$$
(u,(a+bi)v) = a(u,v) + b(u,iv)
$$

On the left
$$
((a + bi)u,v) = a(u,v) + b(iu,v) = a(u,v) - b(u,iv)
$$


Interesting.  So if we just know $(u,v)$ and $(u,iv)$, we can calculate
what any complex scalar does on either side.  It might make sense to keep 
track of both of these together.   Let us define

$$
H(u,v) = \begin{pmatrix} (u,v) \\ (u,iv) \end{pmatrix}
$$

Now I suppose the natural question to ask, is what does a complex scalar 
do do $H$?

$$
H((a+bi)u,v) = \begin{pmatrix} ((a+bi)u,v) \\ ((a+bi)u,iv) \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} a(u,v) - b(u,iv) \\ b(u,v) + a(u,iv) \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} a & -b \\ b & a \end{pmatrix} H(u,v)
$$

$$
H(v, u) = \begin{pmatrix} (v,u) \\ (v,iu) \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} (u,v) \\ -(u,iv) \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix} H(u,v)
$$

*Oh.*

$H$ isn't just two reals.  It's a complex number.  We can redefine it like this.

$$
H(u,v) = (u,v) + i(u,iv)
$$

And now we have
$$
\begin{gather*}
H(zu,v) = zH(u,v) \\
H(v,u) = \overline{H(u,v)}
\end{gather*}
$$

$H$ is a Hermitian inner product.

$H$ is a Hermitian inner product that defines the same norm as $(\cdot,\cdot)$.

The imaginary part of $H$ encodes what $(u,v)$ does when you multiply $u$ or $v$ 
by a complex scalar.

$(u,v)$ is just the real part of $H(u,v)$.

They both contain the same information, just expressed in different ways.

They're the same thing.
